overview: Modern Norway existed before this atlas segment begins in 1914. Its constitution dates to 1814, and the union with Sweden ended in 1905. Democratic participation, wartime occupation, changing homes and offshore industry shaped the following century; its population includes different languages and cultural communities.

periods.title: Independence and wider participation
periods.summary: The Swedish union ended in 1905; voting rights expanded further in 1913 and 1919.

periods.title: Occupation
periods.summary: Nazi German occupation interrupted the operation of democratic institutions.

periods.title: Rebuilding and continued change
periods.summary: Housing, household technology and offshore industry changed work and family life.

items.text: Women gained the same parliamentary voting rights as men in 1913. The remaining exclusion of people receiving poor relief ended in 1919. A single celebrated reform did not remove every barrier at once.

Mænd og Kvinder means “Men and Women.” These words appear in Article 50 as amended in 1913, quoted by the parliamentary archive. The spelling belongs to the document’s historical written language, before later Norwegian spelling reforms.

Nazi Germany invaded on 9 April 1940. Parliament could not function normally under occupation, while the king and government continued in exile. Democratic institutions resumed after liberation in 1945; occupation did not end Norwegian society.

The Sámi Parliament opened in Karasjok in 1989. It represents Sámi interests and develops policies involving language, culture and education. Norway’s history therefore includes Indigenous political institutions as well as the national parliament.

sections.title: The work behind a comfortable home

items.text: A bathroom installed in Oslo in 1930 survived almost unchanged until it entered Norsk Folkemuseum. Its copper hot-water tank could be heated using wood or coke, with an electrical element added at the side. A warm bath required equipment and attention.

The museum reports that in 1973, 31 percent of Norwegian homes still lacked a bathroom and 27 percent lacked a flush toilet. Modernization arrived unevenly; a photograph of one stylish home cannot describe every family’s circumstances.

Electric washing machines reached the Norwegian market in the 1920s but became common only later. In 1973, 72 percent of households had one. Laundry changed from strenuous work with tubs and washboards into a task increasingly shared with machinery.

Alvhild’s Oslo bedsitter in 1982 occupied about ten square metres: loft bed, desk, chairs, a refrigerator and hotplate, plus a toilet with a cold-water sink. The museum reconstructed it partly from her memories, which grew more detailed during the project.

For its 2002 Pakistani-Norwegian home display, the museum selected furnishings with a mother and daughter. They approved carpets, curtains and arrangements. Their participation makes the exhibit evidence of particular family choices, rather than a standard home for all immigrants.

Ekofisk’s oil discovery in 1969 is represented by surprisingly small museum objects: a drill bit and oil taken home in a syrup bottle. These link a major industrial change to the crews and equipment that first encountered the deposit.

Oil brought employment and revenue, but also serious dangers. The Alexander L. Kielland platform disaster killed 123 people in 1980. The petroleum museum treats those losses as part of industrial history alongside technical and economic achievement.

Offshore work drew on existing maritime expertise. Norwegian shipowners began investing in mobile drilling rigs after the 1969 discovery. An industry can grow through adapting accumulated skills, rather than appearing from a single invention.

ending.text: Norway remains a continuing state. The occupation of 1940 to 1945 interrupted democratic government but was followed by its restoration. Constitutional, economic and cultural changes are stages in that history, not separate dates on which the Norwegian people began or ended.
